story: GVEA's first Energy Emergency Alert meets Burgum's Fairbanks data center pitch and ACEP's megawatt ladder in Computing in Place

claims.claim: Golden Valley Electric Association issued its first ever Energy Emergency Alert on October 12th.
claims.verbatim: Yesterday, GVEA issued an Energy Emergency Alert (EEA) for the first time.
claims.notes: Opening of the release, which is dated October 13, 2026, so 'yesterday' is October 12th (a Monday). Corroborated by KUAC ('issued its first energy-emergency alert Monday') and Alaska Public Media ('issued its first-ever energy emergency alert on Monday'). The News-Miner words it as 'first energy alert under a new communication system', so 'first Energy Emergency Alert' is the safe phrasing.

claims.claim: The October 12th alert was a Level 2 alert, triggered when a third GVEA generating unit unexpectedly went offline.
claims.verbatim: What put us into a Level 2 is another unit unexpectedly went offline at the same time.
claims.notes: Body of the GVEA release. KUAC and KTUU both confirm Level 2.

claims.claim: Two GVEA generating units were offline for planned maintenance when the alert was issued.
claims.verbatim: Right now, two of our generating units are offline for planned maintenance.
claims.notes: Corroborated by KTUU: 'two others were undergoing scheduled maintenance before winter weather hits'.

claims.claim: GVEA's alert page defines Level 1, the Energy Advisory, as available generation reserves below 38 MW that are not expected to recover within two hours.
claims.verbatim: Available generation reserves are below 38 MW and are not expected to recover in the next two hours.
claims.notes: Heading on the page is 'LEVEL 1 – Energy Advisory'. DISCREPANCY: the October 13th release defines the levels by backup units, not MW (see C07, C08). Both are GVEA primaries, so the MW wording here is the official threshold and the unit wording is the plain-language gloss. Corroborated by the News-Miner ('available reserves fall below 38 megawatts') and KTUU ('less than 38 megawatts in reserve'). date_of_source is the status stamp shown on the page.

claims.claim: GVEA's alert page defines Level 2, the Energy Watch, as available generation reserves below 15 MW that are not expected to recover within two hours.
claims.verbatim: Available generation reserves are below 15 MW and are not expected to recover within two hours.
claims.notes: Heading is 'LEVEL 2 – Energy Watch'. On the page the line goes on to 'Conserve now and prepare for possible outages'. Corroborated by the News-Miner and KTUU.

claims.claim: GVEA's alert page defines Level 3, the Energy Warning, as generation reserves unavailable and not expected to recover within 30 minutes, which starts its Controlled Load Shed Program.
claims.verbatim: Generation reserves are unavailable and are not expected to recover within 30 minutes.
claims.notes: The line opens with 'CONTROLLED LOAD SHED PROGRAM INITIATED.' and the heading is 'LEVEL 3 – Energy Warning'.

claims.claim: GVEA's news release says Level 1 means its backup power supply is limited to two generation units.
claims.verbatim: Level 1 means our backup power supply is limited to two generation units
claims.notes: This settles the scout disagreement: the release defines levels by backup units and the alert page (C04, C05) by MW. Use the MW thresholds for any numeric comparison. Use this unit framing only with an attribution to the release.

claims.claim: GVEA's news release says Level 2 means its backup power supply is limited to one generation unit.
claims.verbatim: Level 2 means our backup power supply limited to one generation unit
claims.notes: The source drops 'is' in 'supply limited', and the verbatim keeps that as printed.

claims.claim: At Level 3 GVEA would rotate outages of 30 to 60 minutes through designated zones.
claims.verbatim: This involves rotating 30 to 60-minute outages through designated zones.
claims.notes: The alert page says 'Controlled outages are expected to rotate in approximately 30- to 60-minute intervals'. The NUMBER of zones is disputed and is killed (News-Miner says 12, KTUU quotes Bradish saying 13), so say 'designated zones' only.

claims.claim: GVEA says it has experienced conditions consistent with Level 1 and Level 2 alerts on numerous occasions over the past year.
claims.verbatim: Over the past year, GVEA has experienced conditions consistent with Level 1 and Level 2 alerts on numerous occasions
claims.notes: Per the page, those earlier conditions were not formally communicated to members. Attribute it: 'GVEA says'.

claims.claim: GVEA's board approved additional baseload generation with a maximum project cost of $80 million.
claims.verbatim: with a maximum project cost of $80 million.
claims.notes: The full sentence is longer than the fetch tool would quote, so this is its closing clause. A separate fetch summarized the sentence as a Board approval. SOFTEN: write 'up to $80 million', since it's a ceiling and not a spend.

claims.claim: GVEA is evaluating a used LM6000 turbine or an equivalent for that added baseload generation.
claims.verbatim: A used LM6000 turbine, or an equivalent, is being evaluated.
claims.notes: Per the page, it could burn naphtha, or natural gas if gas becomes available in Interior Alaska. That is a plan under evaluation, not a purchase.

claims.claim: GVEA's planned battery energy storage system would provide 70 megawatts of temporary power.
claims.verbatim: The BESS will be able to provide temporary power of 70 megawatts for up to 2 hours
claims.notes: Planned and not yet built, so write 'would'. Unit check: 70 MW for 2 hours is about 140 MWh, which is my arithmetic and not on the page.

claims.claim: GVEA's planned battery would supply that power for up to 2 hours.
claims.verbatim: The BESS will be able to provide temporary power of 70 megawatts for up to 2 hours
claims.notes: Same sentence as C13.

claims.claim: GVEA estimates the battery project will cost about $130 million.
claims.verbatim: estimated to cost about $130 million.
claims.notes: This is an estimate. Keep 'about' or 'estimated'.

claims.claim: After loan forgiveness and tax credits GVEA expects the battery's cost to members to fall to around $18 million.
claims.verbatim: After loan forgiveness and tax credits, the estimated cost to members is reduced to around $18 million.
claims.notes: This is a projection that depends on loan forgiveness and tax credits. SOFTEN: 'GVEA estimates'.

claims.claim: GVEA says it lost access to power from Anchorage area gas plants because of natural gas shortages in Cook Inlet.
claims.verbatim: Since losing access to that power due to natural gas shortages in the Cook Inlet
claims.notes: The verbatim is only the opening clause. The 'Anchorage area gas plants' antecedent comes from the fetch summary of the preceding text. SOFTEN: attribute to GVEA. The release does NOT use the words 'economy energy', 'Southcentral' or 'Intertie'.

claims.claim: By 10:40 a.m. on October 14th GVEA's alert page showed Level 0, normal operations.
claims.verbatim: OCTOBER 14, 2026, 10:40 am
claims.notes: The status heading above the stamp reads 'LEVEL 0 – No Action Needed', and the page says 'GVEA is operating under normal generation conditions.' This is a live page, so it can change. It was the state as fetched on October 16th.

claims.claim: KUAC reported that GVEA was left with a cushion of 15 megawatts of reserve generating capacity when it issued the alert.
claims.verbatim: with only a minimal cushion -- 15 megawatts-- of reserve generating capacity.
claims.notes: Tim Ellis, published October 13, 2026 at 5:22 PM AKDT. The source's double hyphens are kept as printed. SOFTEN: 'according to KUAC'. It is consistent with the 15 MW Level 2 threshold (C05), and that threshold is the safer number to anchor.

claims.claim: KUAC reported the alert would remain in effect through Wednesday, October 14th.
claims.verbatim: The alert will remain in effect through Wednesday.
claims.notes: KTUU also says 'through Wednesday', and Alaska Public Media says 'until Wednesday morning'. The GVEA page showed Level 0 at 10:40 am October 14th (C18).

claims.claim: GVEA spokesperson Ashley Bradish told KUAC the alert is "probably not going to be a one-off."
claims.verbatim: "I do want to prepare the membership that this is probably not going to be a one-off," Bradish said.
claims.notes: Verbatim was confirmed across two fetches. The same article quotes her: 'It is likely that they will be seeing Level 1 and Level 2 alerts,'.

claims.claim: Bradish told KUAC that GVEA's generation situation is "not a quick fix."
claims.verbatim: the generation situation that we're in is not a quick fix, unfortunately.
claims.notes: The News-Miner has a variant from her: 'The generation system we find ourselves in is not going to be a quick fix,'. Quote only the KUAC wording, exactly as printed.

claims.claim: GVEA would not say which unit failed or why, citing new state standards on what utilities may make public, according to Alaska's News Source.
claims.verbatim: citing new state standards for what information utilities are allowed to make public
claims.notes: Alex Bengel, published October 14, 2026 at 5:26 p.m. (the URL path says 10/15). Single source, so attribute it. The same article corroborates the 38 MW and 15 MW thresholds.

claims.claim: GVEA said the problem behind the shortage will take years to fix, according to Alaska Public Media.
claims.verbatim: the problem that caused the shortage will take years to fix.
claims.notes: Shelby Herbert. The article attributes this to 'The utility said'. SOFTEN: attribute it. It is consistent with KTUU's Bradish quote 'not likely to be remedied anytime soon because we do need additional generation.'

claims.claim: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum spoke at a Fairbanks Chamber of Commerce event on the evening of Wednesday, October 14th.
claims.verbatim: Interior Secretary Doug Burgum spent Wednesday evening in Fairbanks,
claims.notes: The same article says 'Burgum spoke at a Fairbanks Chamber of Commerce event'. Wednesday is October 14th (October 12th was the Monday of the alert). Corroborated by KTUU (Adrian Peterson, October 14th, 9:36 PM): 'visited Fairbanks Wednesday, addressing attendees at the 8 Star Event Center'. A scout's 'Tuesday' is wrong.

claims.claim: Burgum told the Fairbanks audience, "We have people knocking on our door that want to drop 10 billion on a data center, and they don't want any tax breaks."
claims.verbatim: "We have people knocking on our door that want to drop 10 billion on a data center, and they don't want any tax breaks," Burgum said.
claims.notes: Identical across three fetches. The printed text says '10 billion' with no dollar sign, so keep it that way. It is Burgum's characterization of unnamed investors, so keep it as a quote and never as a fact.

claims.claim: Alaska Public Media reported that Burgum pitched the Interior as a location for large scale AI data centers.
claims.verbatim: pitching the Interior as a location for large-scale AI data centers and foreign energy investment
claims.notes: ATTRIBUTION FIX: the source is Alaska's News Source (Adrian Peterson), not Alaska Public Media, so render the outlet as KTUU. The same article says 'The visit came days after Golden Valley Electric declared a Level 2 power emergency'.

claims.claim: Alaska has seen proposals for as many as 15 data centers, including on military land, according to Alaska Public Media.
claims.verbatim: Alaska has seen proposals for as many as 15 data centers
claims.notes: The sentence continues 'including on military land near Railbelt and Interior communities.' It is a reporter's tally with no primary list behind it. SOFTEN: 'as many as 15, according to Alaska Public Media'.

claims.claim: In July state officials received more than 500 public comments on a proposed North Slope data center and power plant.
claims.verbatim: In July, state officials received more than 500 public comments on a proposed North Slope data center and power plant.
claims.notes: Background event from July, carried in an in-window article. It is probably the STAK proposal near Prudhoe Bay (C47), but the article does not name it, so don't connect them in prose without hedging.

claims.claim: In August the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly passed a resolution asking the Alaska Legislature to impose a moratorium on data centers.
claims.verbatim: the Fairbanks North Star Borough Assembly passed a resolution to ask the Alaska Legislature to impose a moratorium
claims.notes: The article continues 'on data centers, pending a plan to address community concerns.' It gives no day and no vote count, and the scout's August 27th and 6 to 1 are killed. Say 'in August' only.

claims.claim: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, who attended Burgum's speech, said "I think we should pause."
claims.verbatim: "I think we should pause," Kreiss-Tomkins said.
claims.notes: Identity is given as 'The sole Democratic candidate in Alaska's gubernatorial race, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins' who 'attended Burgum's speech as an audience member'. The quote's context (pause on data centers) is per the article. Don't extend the quote.

claims.claim: The University of Alaska Fairbanks Alaska Center for Energy and Power prepared Computing in Place, a conversation guide on data centers for Alaskans, dated October 2026.
claims.verbatim: COMPUTING IN PLACE A Conversation Guide on Data Centers for Alaskans, by Alaskans 1 of 61 Prepared by the Alaska Center for Energy and Power October 2026
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Cover page, from the text layer at /home/user/alaskaaicarousels/out/2026-10-15/pdf/cip_flat.txt. The suggested citation is 'UAF/ACEP/TP-08-001'. Zenodo record date is October 6th (C35). Background date, before the window, but announced in window (C34).

claims.claim: The guide runs 61 pages and its lead author is Leasi Vanessa Lee Raymond.
claims.verbatim: Lead author: Leasi Vanessa Lee Raymond
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: The page count rests on the '1 of 61' through '61 of 61' footers. The navigation lists page numbers up to 65, a mismatch inside the document, so prefer 'about 60 pages' if the count is shown. Zenodo lists Raymond with a 'Concordia University' affiliation, so don't print an affiliation. The UAF release says Raymond 'leads the project'. Split from the page count if the gate wants strict atomicity.

claims.claim: UAF announced the guide on October 14th, saying it was developed by the Alaska Center for Energy and Power.
claims.verbatim: was developed by the Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: UAF news is dated October 14, 2026. The ACEP copy at https://www.uaf.edu/acep/news/2026/new-guide-helps-alaskans-shape-data-center-conversations.php is dated October 11, 2026, so the first announcement was arguably October 11th.

claims.claim: The guide was published on Zenodo on October 6th under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 license.
claims.verbatim: Published October 6, 2026
claims.source_outlet: Zenodo (UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power record)
claims.notes: The license shows as 'Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International'. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23175112.

claims.claim: The guide's work relates to Office of Naval Research award N00014-22-1-2049.
claims.verbatim: This work relates to the Department of Navy award N00014-22-1-2049 issued by the Office of Naval Research.
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Acknowledgements, page 1. Zenodo's funding line matches: 'Alaska Regional Collaboration for Technology, Innovation, and Commercialization (ARCTIC) II N00014-22-1-2049'.

claims.claim: ACEP convened a two day discussion of Alaska leaders in June 2026 that informed the guide.
claims.verbatim: in June 2026, the Alaska Center for Energy and Power (ACEP) convened a two-day discussion
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: 'How This Conversation Guide Was Created', page 7. Per the guide it was held under the Chatham House Rule. If the claim is shown on a slide, drop the year (June).

claims.claim: The guide says a small facility supporting a hospital or Tribal government is different from a hyperscale facility serving global customers.
claims.verbatim: A small facility supporting a hospital or Tribal government is different from a hyperscale facility serving global customers.
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Executive Summary, page 5. Exact match.

claims.claim: The guide frames four questions, namely what computing Alaska needs, what resources should support it, who should control it, and what if anything Alaskans want to provide to the rest of the world.
claims.verbatim: What computing does Alaska need? What resources should we use to support it? Who should control it? And what, if anything, do Alaskans want to provide to the rest of the world?
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Executive Summary, page 5. Exact match.

claims.claim: The guide sizes an edge data center at approximately 0.1 to 0.5 MW in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Small (approximately 0.1–0.5 MW in AK)
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Edge Data Center profile, page 29. The en dash is the source's own and stays in the verbatim. Slide copy must render it as 'to'.

claims.claim: The guide cites the Alaska Department of Transportation and Public Facilities containerized edge data center, used to store drone imagery, as an Alaska example of the edge type.
claims.verbatim: Alaska Department of Transportation & Public Facilities’ (AK DOT&PF) containerized edge data center is used for storing drone imagery data collected in remote locations
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Page 10. The verbatim keeps the source's curly apostrophe. Inside the guide, page 29 calls it 'AK Department of Transportation and Public Works data center'. Use the DOT&PF name from page 10.

claims.claim: The guide sizes an enterprise data center at approximately 0.5 to 10 MW in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Small to medium (Approximately 0.5–10 MW in AK)
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Enterprise Data Center profile, page 27. The en dash is in the source.

claims.claim: The guide names the University of Alaska data center and the Providence Hospital data center as enterprise examples in Alaska today.
claims.verbatim: University of Alaska data center ● Providence Hospital data center
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Page 27, under 'Examples in Alaska today'. The caption there reads 'The University of Alaska’s Butrovich building (lower left) houses an example of an enterprise data center.'

claims.claim: The guide sizes a co-location data center at approximately 0.5 to 100 MW.
claims.verbatim: Small to medium (approximately 0.5–100 MW)
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Co-location profile, page 31. Unlike the other four types it carries no 'in AK' qualifier. The guide's Alaska co-location example is Cordova Electric's hydro-powered facility (page 10).

claims.claim: The guide sizes a cloud data center at 50 to 100 or more MW, or even gigawatts, in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Medium to large (50–100+ MW or even GW in AK)
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Cloud profile, page 32. The size band is identical to hyperscale's (C48), and the guide separates the two by infrastructure intensity: 'generally smaller and less infrastructure-intensive than hyperscale AI campuses'.

claims.claim: The guide says no large commercial cloud providers currently operate cloud regions in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: No large commercial cloud providers currently operate cloud regions in Alaska.
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Cloud profile, page 32. This is the guide's statement as of October 2026.

claims.claim: The guide says no operational hyperscale facilities currently exist in Alaska and cites the STAK proposal on the North Slope as a proposed example.
claims.verbatim: Proposed AI and hyperscale campus developments, such as the STAK proposal on the North Slope. No operational hyperscale facilities currently exist in Alaska.
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Hyperscale profile, page 33. Page 10 describes it as 'The proposed hyperscale data center near Prudhoe Bay from STAK Energy'.

claims.claim: The guide sizes a hyperscale data center at 50 to 100 or more MW, or even gigawatts, in Alaska.
claims.verbatim: Large to mega-scale (50–100+ MW or even GW in AK)
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Hyperscale profile, page 33. Also there: 'with power demands measured in tens to hundreds of megawatts and, increasingly, gigawatts'. The comparison with GVEA (a 50 MW floor above GVEA's 38 MW Level 1 line) is the deck's arithmetic and not a claim in any source. Present it as a juxtaposition, not as a finding.

claims.claim: The guide's question for the hyperscale type is "How much change is our community prepared to absorb?"
claims.verbatim: How much change is our community prepared to absorb?
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Hyperscale profile 'Makes us ask', page 33. It is repeated in Worksheet 4.

claims.claim: The guide says hyperscale AI or cloud scale projects on the Railbelt may require significant new power generation and transmission beyond what exists today.
claims.verbatim: Even so, projects at the scale of hyperscale AI or cloud computing may require signiﬁcant new power generation and transmission investments beyond what exists for the community today.
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Railbelt subsection of the guide's size section, page 20. 'signiﬁcant' contains the PDF ligature U+FB01, kept as extracted. Normalize it to 'fi' if the gate does an ASCII compare. The section title contains a banned word, so don't name the section in copy.

claims.claim: The guide says large scale data centers are unlikely to be economically feasible in remote communities running diesel powered microgrids without transformative investment.
claims.verbatim: large-scale data centers are unlikely to be economically feasible in remote communities running diesel-powered microgrids
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: Off-the-Road System subsection, page 20. The sentence continues 'without transformative investments in generation, transmission, telecommunications, and other supporting infrastructure'.

claims.claim: The guide says Alaska's energy limits come from the cost and complexity of developing and connecting its resources rather than from a lack of resources.
claims.verbatim: Alaska’s energy limitations are not due to the availability of resources, but rather to the cost and complexity of developing them, connecting them to markets, and creating enough demand to support long-term investment.
claims.source_outlet: UAF Alaska Center for Energy and Power
claims.notes: 'Is Alaska Energy Rich or Energy Poor?', page 21. The same section says 'By a different measure, Alaska is one of the most energy- and mineral-rich places in the world.' It also says 'In most parts of Alaska, those types of demands could change the entire region’s economics and infrastructure.'

claims.claim: A Department of Energy project will build approximately 223 miles of new transmission line connecting Beluga and Healy.
claims.verbatim: Approximately 223 miles of new transmission line connecting Beluga and Healy will be built.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND, dated October 5th, before the window. The line connects Beluga and Healy, not Fairbanks.

claims.claim: The Beluga to Healy line combines up to $150 million in Defense Production Act funding with $268 million in non-federal funding.
claims.verbatim: combines up to $150 million in DPA funding with $268 million in non-federal funding.
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. Sanity check: 150 + 268 = 418, which matches the page's 'planned total investment of $418 million in Alaska's grid'.

claims.claim: Construction of the second intertie isn't expected until after 2030, according to the Alaska Beacon.
claims.verbatim: Construction isn't expected until after 2030.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Anchorage Daily News
claims.notes: BACKGROUND. James Brooks, Alaska Beacon, published October 8, 2026 (the URL path says 10/07). This is a projection. SOFTEN: 'isn't expected until after 2030'. The article does not mention GVEA or data centers.

claims.claim: The Alaska Senate Resources Committee voted to subpoena Natural Resources Commissioner John Crowther over a proposed land transfer to AIDEA.
claims.verbatim: after legislators on the Senate Resources Committee voted Wednesday to issue a subpoena.
claims.notes: Eric Stone, October 15, 2026, 5:06 PM AKDT. 'Wednesday' is October 14th. No vote count is reported. DOCKET LEAD. No primary (a legislature record) was fetched, so this is single-source secondary.

claims.claim: DNR confirmed that Commissioner Crowther will appear at a Senate hearing on October 26th.
claims.verbatim: The department confirmed Thursday that Commissioner John Crowther would appear at a hearing on Oct. 26
claims.notes: DOCKET LEAD. This is a scheduled event, so write 'is scheduled to appear'.

claims.claim: The proposed transfer to AIDEA covers roughly 20,000 acres near the Mat-Su community of Houston.
claims.verbatim: roughly 20,000-acre proposed land transfer
claims.notes: The article also says 'approximately 30 square miles near the Mat-Su community of Houston'. Sanity check: 20,000 acres is about 31 square miles, so they agree. It says the site could host 'an industrial park that could include data centers', and that AIDEA's director called a data center there 'implausible'.

claims.claim: Governor Dunleavy's office had not let Crowther attend the Senate Resources hearing on October 8th, according to Alaska Public Media.
claims.verbatim: would not say why the governor didn't allow Crowther to attend the Oct. 8 meeting.
claims.notes: SOFTEN: the article implies he was absent but frames it as permission not given. Use this framing, not 'he did not appear'.

claims.claim: DNR's Division of Oil and Gas issued a preliminary written finding on October 13th for a Kenai Loop gas storage lease.
claims.verbatim: Notice of Issuance of the Kenai Loop Gas Field Storage Lease Preliminary Written Finding of the Director and Request for Comments
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Notice publish date 10/13/2026. The finding PDF's cover is dated October 13, 2026. DOCKET LEAD, primary.

claims.claim: The preliminary finding concludes that a Kenai Loop gas storage lease to ENSTAR would best serve the state's interest.
claims.verbatim: for the purposes of gas storage to ENSTAR would best serve the state’s interest.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Page 1, last sentence of the Introduction. Transcribed from the rendered page image, because the PDF has no text layer for WebFetch. ENSTAR Natural Gas Company, LLC and Hilcorp Cook Inlet, LLC both applied, and the page 17 conclusion says 'Hilcorp’s application was considered to be insufficient'. The finding is preliminary and signed by Director Haley Paine, with lease ADL 394695. Petroleum News (Kristen Nelson, issue dated October 18th) corroborates.

claims.claim: Comments on the Kenai Loop preliminary finding must be received by 5 p.m. on November 13th.
claims.verbatim: Comments must be received on or before 5:00 p.m., November 13, 2026,
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Petroleum News says the same: 'Comments are due by 5 p.m. Nov. 13.'

claims.claim: ENSTAR's Kenai Loop proposal would hold a total working gas volume of about 20.5 Bcf with about 8 Bcf of cushion gas.
claims.verbatim: In either case, the total working gas volume would be about 20.5 Bcf and the cushion gas volumes would be approximately 8 Bcf.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska DNR Division of Oil and Gas
claims.notes: Page 16, transcribed from the page image. Under a full nine-well build the same paragraph gives 150 MMscf/D peak withdrawal. Petroleum News matches with 20.5 bcf and 8 bcf.

claims.claim: More than 1,500 people were forced from their homes by Typhoon Halong in October 2025, KYUK reported.
claims.verbatim: More than 1,500 people were forced from their homes.
claims.notes: Evan Erickson, October 12, 2026. 'October 2025' comes from the article's summary line ('In October 2025, daily life in dozens of Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta communities was suddenly interrupted'). Runner-up story.

claims.claim: State officials say 675 homes across the region still need repairs a year after Halong.
claims.verbatim: Zidek said that a total of 675 homes across the region still need repairs.
claims.notes: Jeremy Zidek is with the state Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management.

claims.claim: FEMA has paid out more than $100 million to people affected by the storm over the past year, according to KYUK.
claims.verbatim: FEMA has paid out more than $100 million to people impacted by the storm
claims.notes: The figure covers individual, housing and other needs assistance.

claims.claim: The state's request for FEMA funding to replace 219 severely damaged homes in Kipnuk was denied, KYUK reported.
claims.verbatim: permanent housing construction funding to replace 219 homes severely damaged in Kipnuk
claims.notes: The denial is in the same sentence but outside the fetched verbatim fragment, and the reasons are unclear per the article. SOFTEN: 'KYUK reported'.

claims.claim: In Kipnuk 90 percent of buildings were damaged or destroyed by the storm.
claims.verbatim: In Kipnuk, 90% of buildings were damaged or destroyed
claims.notes: Per the article, nearly all of Kipnuk's 974 residents evacuated.

claims.claim: Taiwan's economic affairs ministry said it will invest up to $4.4 billion in the Alaska LNG pipeline project.
claims.verbatim: it will invest up to $4.4 billion in the pipeline project.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: James Brooks, October 15, 2026. The ministry spoke Wednesday. It is not final, and terms 'will be determined through subsequent negotiations'. SOFTEN: 'up to', 'nearing'.

claims.claim: Taiwan could sign a heads of agreement with preliminary sale terms as soon as the following week, according to sources cited by the Alaska Beacon.
claims.verbatim: Taiwan could sign a document with preliminary sale terms, called a heads of agreement document, as soon as next week.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: This is a projection from unnamed sources. SOFTEN heavily.

claims.claim: Glenfarne currently owns 75 percent of the Alaska LNG pipeline project.
claims.verbatim: Seventy-five percent of the pipeline project is currently owned by the private developer Glenfarne,
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The state-controlled Alaska Gasline Development Corp. owns the rest.

claims.claim: Official estimates put the Alaska LNG project's cost between $44.5 billion and $54.5 billion.
claims.verbatim: Official estimates state that the project will cost between $44.5 billion to $54.5 billion.
claims.source_outlet: Alaska Beacon via Alaska Public Media
claims.notes: The article notes that unofficial estimates exceed $65 billion. The pipeline would carry '20 million metric tons of natural gas per year from the North Slope to an export terminal on Cook Inlet.'

DNR preliminary finding favouring ENSTAR for the Kenai Loop gas storage lease (docket, C60 to C63)

killed.claim: GVEA's Level 3 rotating outages run across 12 zones (or 13 zones).
killed.why: Disputed. The News-Miner says 'GVEA's 12 zones' and KTUU quotes Bradish saying 'those 13 different zones'. Neither GVEA page states a count, so use 'designated zones'.

killed.claim: The FNSB Assembly voted 6 to 1 on August 27th for priorities including a data center moratorium.
killed.why: The Alaska Public Media article says only 'in August' and gives no day and no vote count, and no other fetched page supports it. The moratorium resolution survives as C30 without date or tally.

killed.claim: Burgum's remarks or the article reference S. 5653.
killed.why: The bill number is not in the article's visible text. It appears only as a congress.gov hyperlink behind 'He said he hopes Congress will pass legislation to roll back environmental regulations after the midterm elections.' A link target is not a printed claim.
Contradicted. Both Alaska Public Media and KTUU say Wednesday (October 14th).

killed.claim: GVEA's release discusses economy energy purchases from Southcentral over the Intertie.
killed.why: Not on the release. It mentions only losing access to Anchorage-area gas power due to Cook Inlet shortages (C17).

killed.claim: GVEA's news release defines alert levels in megawatts.
killed.why: False as worded. The release defines them by backup generation units (C07, C08), and the MW thresholds come from the alert page (C04, C05). Both survive with the right source.

killed.claim: Crowther did not appear at the October 8th hearing.
killed.why: Not stated directly. The article says the governor's office did not allow him to attend. Replaced by the softened C59.

killed.claim: Raymond said the guide 'is a tool for asking better questions, bringing the right people into the conversation'.
killed.why: Only surfaced in a summarizing fetch of the UAF release and not reconfirmed verbatim on a second fetch. Quote her only via the PDF sentence in C38.

killed.claim: Raymond is affiliated with Concordia University.
killed.why: Zenodo metadata says so but conflicts with the guide and UAF releases (ACEP). It is unreliable metadata and not used.

killed.claim: Burgum said 'you convert electricity into intelligence, you make money.'
killed.why: Seen in a single summarizing fetch of KTUU and not reconfirmed verbatim. Excluded to keep named-person quotes to double-confirmed strings.

killed.claim: Petroleum News reported the Kenai Loop finding (as the primary citation).
killed.why: Not killed as a fact, but demoted. Its issue date (October 18th) is after the run date, so the DNR notice and finding PDF are cited instead (C60 to C63).

killed.claim: The Beluga to Healy line reaches Fairbanks.
killed.why: The DOE page says it connects Beluga and Healy and does not mention Fairbanks.
